newsitem.title: BURUNDI: U.S. envoy arrives in Burundi, to meet Buyoya.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy arrives in Burundi, to meet Buyoya.

text.p: The U.S. presidential envoy on Burundi, Howard Wolpe, flew into the capital of the sanctions-hit country on Sunday and will meet military leader Pierre Buyoya on Monday, a senior official said.

Wolpe went straight from the airport to the U.S. ambassador's residence in Bujumbura where ex-president Sylvestre Ntibantungya took refuge on July 23, two days before he was overthrown in a coup by the Tutsi-dominated army.
"We expect Mr Wolpe to meet the president (Buyoya) on Monday," Major Buyoya's spokesman, Jean-Luc Ndizeye, told Reuters.
Ndizeye said the military regime expected Wolpe to insist on immediate talks with Hutu rebel groups and specifically with Leonard Nyangoma, head of the largest armed faction.
"But we can't do that. Buyoya can't just go and shake Nyangoma's hand tomorrow," Ndizeye said.

Regional countries, including all of landlocked Burundi's neighbours, imposed a total economic and trade embargo on July 31 in protest against the army coup. The sanctions are biting hard, blocking coffee exports and sending the price of basic commodities and oil rocketing.

The regional leaders demanded that Buyoya meet three main conditions before sanctions are eased. He has agreed to restore the national assembly and has unbanned political parties but has so far failed to meet Nyangoma or other exiled rebel leaders from Burundi's Hutu majority.
The military regime says the rebels must first renounce the "ideology of genocide" and stop killing civilians. "But we are not saying they must surrender their arms as a pre-condition," Ndizeye said.

He linked Wolpe's visit to U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's first African tour between October 7-15. Christopher will not come to Burundi but will meet leaders of key pro-sanctions nations in Arusha, Tanzania.

Ndizeye said he expected Buyoya to be invited to a regional summit on Burundi which he thought would be held in Arusha on October 12. Regional leaders have so far refused to see Buyoya at summit level but their sanctions committee recommended last week that he be "invited to be available" at their next summit.

About 150,000 people have been killed in the past three years of ethnic war in Burundi. There is no accurate figure for current losses because insecurity in the tiny country of six million people prevents aid workers from moving freely.

Wolpe was appointed by President Bill Clinton before the coup to underline U.S. concern over Burundi's dangerous drift, two years after the genocide of up to one million people in neighbouring Rwanda.
Wolpe met Ntibantunganya for lunch on Sunday at the residence. "It was a small, informal affair," one of the guests said.
Buyoya's regime will allow the ex-president to go abroad but insists he must first leave the embassy and go to his private residence.
"We will not accept that he leaves Burundi straight from the U.S. embassy residence," Ndizeye said.
